services.name: Drain Cleaning
services.title: Drain Cleaning Chicago, IL | The Chicago Plumber
services.meta: The Chicago Plumber provides drain cleaning in Chicago, IL, checking sinks, tubs, showers, floor drains, and backed-up lines to locate blockages.
services.blurb: We clear and inspect blocked drains across Chicago, Cicero, Stickney, and Oak Park.

paragraphs: We hear about sinks that gurgle, tubs that hold dirty water, and floor drains that give off a sewer smell. We start at the fixture where the water is slow or backing up, then check whether the blockage is in the trap, the branch pipe, or a larger drain route farther along the line.

We check the sink bowl, shower tray, tub drain, and nearby fixtures because water can appear in the wrong place when two drains share a branch. Grease, soap residue, hair, paper, and food scraps can narrow a pipe gradually, while a solid obstruction can stop water suddenly. We also look for water around the cabinet base, floor drain, or cleanout cap before clearing a line.

We can usually schedule an isolated slow sink or tub drain before it becomes a complete stoppage, especially when no water is escaping from the fixture. We do not recommend waiting on a backup at a floor drain, shower, or lower fixture, because wastewater can overflow onto flooring and the blockage can affect additional drains on the same pipe.

sections.heading: Gurgling and sewer smell
paragraphs: We regularly hear customers describe a sink that drains slowly, a toilet that makes a bubbling sound when the shower runs, a shower tray filling around their feet, or a floor drain with a sewer smell. A kitchen sink may also back up when a dishwasher drains, while a laundry standpipe can spill water when the washer pumps out.

We treat a gurgle, standing water, and a sewer odor as different clues rather than one diagnosis. A gurgle can point to air moving past a partial blockage, while a recurring odor may come from a dry trap, residue inside the pipe, or a drain that is not moving water as it should. Water rising through a basement floor drain can indicate that the restriction is farther from the fixture than a simple sink trap.

We inspect the pipe route before deciding what needs clearing because similar symptoms can come from separate faults. A hair-packed shower drain, a grease-filled kitchen branch, and a blockage beyond a cleanout require different work and parts, even when each one starts with water draining slowly.

sections.heading: Drain inspection callout
paragraphs: During a drain inspection callout, we identify the affected fixture, run water where it is safe to do so, and check the trap, stopper, strainer, and accessible pipe connections. We ask which fixture was used when the problem began, then compare the water level and flow at nearby sinks, tubs, or floor drains. A sink branch is commonly 1 1/2 inches in diameter, while tub, shower, and laundry drains are often 2 inches, so the fixture and pipe size help us choose the right approach.

We inspect an accessible cleanout for evidence of a restriction farther along the route and assess the pipe material before using a cable or other clearing tool. Older cast-iron pipe can collect scale on its interior wall, while plastic pipe may have a different fitting layout and access point. If we open a trap, we inspect the slip nuts, washers, and trap arm, replacing a damaged washer or worn component when the connection cannot be reassembled properly.

A basic trap and fixture check can take roughly 15 to 30 minutes once the cabinet or drain opening is accessible. We can often clear an accessible branch-drain obstruction and test the fixture during the same visit; a camera inspection, difficult cleanout access, or work beyond the reachable branch may need a separate booking after we establish where the blockage sits.

sections.heading: Cleanout access and pipe material
paragraphs: The cleanout location, the pipe material, and the route from the fixture all affect the scope of drain work. A cleanout behind a finished wall, beneath stored boxes, or in a tight crawl space takes more preparation than one beside an open basement wall. We also need to account for a cleanout plug that has seized or a trap connection that cannot be opened without replacing a washer or fitting.

Older cast-iron pipe may have scale, rough joints, or corrosion that changes how we approach a blockage, while PVC and ABS fittings can have different access limits. Grease in a kitchen branch, hair in a shower trap, and debris at a floor drain do not clear the same way, and a recurring backup may call for inspection beyond the first accessible opening.

If the work shows a damaged pipe, a failed fitting, or a route that requires alteration rather than clearing, the job can involve ordered parts and, where required, building or municipal sign-off. We explain the condition of the pipe and the access issue before moving from a straightforward drain clearing to additional work.

sections.heading: Fixture and cleanout location
paragraphs: Before calling, we ask that you note which room and fixture is slow, blocked, or backing up, such as the kitchen sink, first-floor tub, basement floor drain, or laundry standpipe. We also need to know whether another sink, toilet, shower, or appliance causes water to rise at that fixture.

If the affected drain is at a kitchen sink with a garbage disposal, we can use the model number from the plate on the disposal housing to prepare for related access issues. We ask whether water is standing in the bowl or tray now, whether a cabinet, basement wall, or crawl space gives access to the pipe, and whether you can see a cleanout cap.

We can use those fixture and access details to send the right drain-clearing equipment for the route we expect to inspect. Call The Chicago Plumber at (847) 809-2341 before a backed-up floor drain or shower drain allows wastewater to spread across the floor.

services.name: Leak Repair
services.title: Leak Repair | The Chicago Plumber | Chicago, IL
services.meta: The Chicago Plumber finds and repairs leaks in pipes, ceilings, cabinets, and walls across Chicago, IL. Call with the fixture, room, and leak location.
services.blurb: We trace and repair pipe, ceiling, cabinet, and wall leaks across Chicago.

paragraphs: A puddle spreading from a kitchen cabinet and a brown ring appearing on a hallway ceiling both get called a leak, but they are not the same repair. From the hallway, a floor puddle usually points toward a fixture connection, supply tube, shutoff valve, or drain nearby. A ceiling stain can be caused by a pipe above, a shower connection, or water that has traveled along framing from another room.

We trace both visible water and hidden moisture. From 210 N Racine Ave, we cover leak repairs in Chicago, Cicero, Stickney, and Oak Park, checking the fixture, pipe route, cabinet base, ceiling area, and nearby valves before opening a wall or replacing a fitting.

An active drip, wet drywall, growing ceiling stain, or water reaching a cabinet should not wait because water can move through insulation, framing, and flooring after the original leak starts. A dry stain that has not changed can be scheduled for inspection, but we still need to determine whether the pipe or connection behind it remains wet.

sections.heading: Water under the sink
paragraphs: We hear calls about water under the sink, a drip through the ceiling, a hissing sound in the wall, a wet spot beside the toilet, and a cabinet floor that keeps getting damp. Water that appears only while a fixture runs can point to a drain joint, overflow, trap, or discharge connection. Water that collects while every fixture is off can point instead to a pressurized supply line, angle stop, valve body, or appliance connection.

A stain on a ceiling may be old water, condensation, or an active pipe leak, while a damp cabinet can come from a loose compression nut, a split supply tube, or water running down from the countertop. These symptoms can look alike from the room, but the failed part, access needed, and repair scope can be very different once we inspect the pipe and fixture.

sections.heading: Leak inspection and test
paragraphs: At the callout, we first identify where water is appearing and check whether the source is above, behind, or below that spot. We inspect supply lines, shutoff valves, trap joints, pipe fittings, fixture bases, access panels, and visible framing. A moisture meter helps us compare the wet area with surrounding drywall or cabinet material, while a pressure check and water-meter observation can help distinguish a pressurized pipe leak from water released only when a fixture is used.

Initial tracing commonly takes between thirty and sixty minutes when the pipe and connections are accessible. We can usually replace an exposed supply tube, compression fitting, washer, shutoff valve, or damaged section of accessible pipe during the same visit when the required material is available. If the source sits behind tile, inside a finished ceiling, below a slab, or in a specialty valve that needs an ordered part, we isolate the leak where possible and schedule the opening, replacement, and wall-access work separately.

sections.heading: Shutoff valves, pipe age, wall access
paragraphs: The condition of the shutoff valve, the age and material of the pipe, and the route to the wet area all affect the scope of a leak repair. A recent leak at an exposed braided supply line or cabinet connection is generally more direct to reach than a pinhole in aging copper behind a tiled shower wall. Corroded threaded fittings, brittle plastic connectors, and previous patchwork can require more disassembly before we can install a sound replacement.

A shutoff valve that will not close can add work because the water supply must be controlled before a fitting is removed. Access through an existing panel, unfinished basement ceiling, or open cabinet keeps the repair focused on the pipe; finished drywall, plaster, tile, or built-in cabinetry can require careful opening and later restoration. Specialty cartridges, uncommon valve bodies, and parts that must be ordered extend the job beyond the initial visit, and some building work may require a sign-off after the plumbing repair.

sections.heading: Fixture model and access panel
paragraphs: Before calling, note the room, the fixture, and the exact place where water is showing, such as under a vanity, below a ceiling light, beside a toilet base, or at a pipe in the basement. Tell us whether water appears while the fixture is running, after it is shut off, or when no fixture has been used. If the leaking item is a specialty valve, filter housing, or faucet, the make and model from a label on the valve body, cabinet paperwork, or installation booklet can help us identify the correct part. Let us know the approximate age of the fitting and whether there is an access panel, open cabinet, basement ceiling, or finished wall around the pipe. Call The Chicago Plumber at (847) 809-2341 before water spreads farther into drywall, flooring, insulation, or cabinet wood.

services.name: Toilet Repair
services.title: Toilet Repair | The Chicago Plumber | Chicago, IL
services.meta: The Chicago Plumber repairs running, leaking, weak-flushing, and clogged toilets across Chicago, IL. Call with your tank model and fixture symptoms.
services.blurb: Running, leaking, or weak-flushing toilet repairs across Chicago.

paragraphs: A toilet that runs for a minute after flushing may seem like a small tank problem. After a week, the fill valve can cycle repeatedly and send water through the overflow tube. After a month, a worn flapper or misadjusted chain can keep the tank refilling long enough to show up on the water bill.

A slow flush can also change from an occasional inconvenience to a bowl that will not clear paper or waste. Repeated partial flushes leave debris in the trapway, while water around the base can soak the flooring, loosen the toilet bolts, and damage the wax ring beneath the bowl.

We repair toilet tanks, bowls, fill valves, flush valves, flappers, handles, supply lines, and base seals throughout Chicago, Cicero, Stickney, and Oak Park. A handle that needs a minor adjustment may wait briefly, but a running tank, leaking base, or bowl that threatens to overflow should not wait because water can reach the floor, subfloor, and adjacent room.

sections.heading: Running water and weak flush
paragraphs: “My toilet keeps running” often means water is passing a flapper at the bottom of the tank, although a fill valve that will not shut off can create the same sound. You may hear the tank refill every few minutes, see water entering the overflow tube, or notice ripples in the bowl when nobody has used the fixture.

“The toilet will not flush” can describe a loose trip lever, a broken lift chain, a handle that has stopped catching, or a tank with too little water for a full flush. A weak flush, a bowl that rises before draining, and a toilet that needs two or three flushes are different symptoms, even when they occur at the same fixture.

Water on the bathroom floor may come from the supply connection, tank bolts, a cracked tank, condensation, or the seal below the bowl. A sewer-like odor around the base, a rocking bowl, and stains on the ceiling below also point to different parts of the toilet assembly.

These faults can look similar from outside the tank, but the failed part, the labor involved, and the materials needed are not the same. We inspect the bowl, tank, shutoff valve, and floor connection before identifying the repair.

sections.heading: Tank and bowl inspection
paragraphs: At a toilet inspection, we start by flushing the fixture and watching the tank fill, the flapper seat, the overflow tube, and the bowl water level. We check the handle, lift chain, fill valve, supply line, tank bolts, and shutoff valve for movement, corrosion, or active water. A tank check and adjustment commonly takes about 20 to 40 minutes when the issue is visible and the fixture is accessible.

We can test the water pressure at the nearby supply and check whether the stop valve fully closes before removing a fill valve or supply line. Residential plumbing pressure is commonly kept in the range of 40 to 60 psi; unusually high pressure can shorten the life of rubber seals and fill-valve components. We also check for water at the base and test whether the bowl shifts against the floor.

Flappers, fill valves, handles, chains, and standard supply connectors are often replaced during the same visit when the correct part is available. Common flush valves are sized around 2 or 3 inches, and the tank model determines which seal, gasket, and hardware fit. A cracked bowl, damaged flange, seized shutoff valve, concealed floor damage, or a special-order tank part may require a return visit after the needed material or approval is arranged.

sections.heading: Tank age and shutoff valve
paragraphs: The age and make of the toilet tank affect the repair because older flush valves, proprietary flappers, discontinued handles, and corroded tank bolts may not match current replacement parts. A common fill valve or flapper is usually a more direct repair than a specialty cartridge or a part that must be ordered for a particular tank model.

Access at the shutoff valve and around the bowl also changes the work involved. A toilet in a tight water closet, a valve behind cabinetry, or a supply line blocked by a pedestal sink can take more setup and testing than an open bathroom fixture. If the shutoff valve has seized, leaks when turned, or will not fully stop the water, that valve may need attention before the tank component can be changed.

A bowl that rocks can point to loose closet bolts, a failing wax ring, uneven tile, or trouble at the floor flange. Resetting a bowl requires removing it from the flange and checking the condition of the seal and floor surface, rather than simply tightening a bolt.

Some buildings require management access, water shutoff coordination, or sign-off before work at a shared plumbing connection can proceed. We explain the condition of the tank, bowl, valve, and floor connection so you can see which part of the repair is driving the scope.

sections.heading: Tank model and bowl location
paragraphs: Before calling, look inside the tank lid or along the back wall of the tank for the manufacturer name and model number; many toilets print or stamp this information on the porcelain. Tell us which bathroom holds the fixture, such as the first-floor powder room or an upstairs hall bath, especially when the toilet is above a finished ceiling.

If water is running now, note whether it enters the overflow tube, leaks from the tank, or appears around the bowl base after a flush. Let us know if the handle is loose, the bowl is clogged, or the toilet rocks on the tile, since those symptoms point to different parts and tools.

A photo of the tank interior, fill valve, flapper, and shutoff valve can help identify the likely fitting before the visit. Mention any cabinet, pedestal sink, or restricted space beside the bowl that affects access to the supply line or closet bolts.
Call The Chicago Plumber at (847) 809-2341 with the tank model and the bathroom location; a running tank or leaking base can worsen from wasted water to damaged flooring when it is left in place.

services.name: Water Heater Repair
services.h1: Water Heater Repair in Chicago, IL
services.title: Water Heater Repair | The Chicago Plumber | Chicago, IL
services.meta: The Chicago Plumber handles water heater faults in Chicago, IL, from no hot water and pilot issues to leaks, elements, valves, and tank checks.
services.blurb: Water heater diagnosis and repair for no hot water, leaks, and pilot problems.

paragraphs: Turning the thermostat up, checking the electrical panel, or looking at the status light on a gas control is a sensible first step when the shower goes cold. A tripped breaker, a thermostat set too low, or a pilot that has gone out can sometimes explain the problem. We check those simple causes first because they can point directly to the failed part without taking apart the tank.

Those checks usually stop being useful when the heater has power or fuel but still produces cold, rusty, or short-lived hot water. A bad heating element, failed thermostat, worn thermocouple, damaged dip tube, or sediment at the bottom of the tank needs testing at the appliance rather than another adjustment at the wall. We trace the fault through the control, wiring, valves, burner, and tank connections before recommending a repair.

A water heater problem should not be left alone when water is collecting beneath the tank, the relief valve is discharging, the burner will not stay lit, or there is a gas smell near the appliance. A tank leak can spread into flooring and framing, while a failed temperature or pressure component can put stress on the tank itself.

sections.heading: No hot water or tank rumbling
paragraphs: We regularly hear, “There is no hot water,” “the water only stays hot for a few minutes,” or “the heater is making a popping noise.” No hot water can come from an electric element, a thermostat, a breaker, a gas valve, an igniter, a thermocouple, or a pilot assembly. Hot water that runs out quickly often points toward an element, dip tube, burner, or sediment issue instead.

A rumbling, popping, or kettle-like sound from the lower tank often happens when mineral sediment collects around the heat source. The burner or electric element then heats through that buildup, and the tank may take longer to recover after a shower or dishwasher cycle. We inspect the drain connection, heating components, and tank condition to separate sediment noise from a failing part.

Water around the base, a wet fitting above the tank, rusty water at the hot faucet, or a relief valve that drips are different symptoms again. A loose connector, aging supply line, drain valve, expansion tank, temperature and pressure relief valve, or corroded tank seam can all leave water near the heater. The location of the moisture matters as much as the amount.

These signs can look alike from across a utility room, but they do not lead to the same repair. We identify the actual failed component before discussing the work, since a serviceable valve, a replaceable control, and a leaking tank involve different materials and different labor.

sections.heading: Tank and burner inspection
paragraphs: We start the callout by checking the model plate, fuel type, tank connections, shutoff valves, relief valve, drain valve, and visible corrosion. We verify the water temperature at a faucet, check the appliance setting, and look for active seepage at the top and bottom of the tank. A basic diagnosis commonly takes thirty to sixty minutes, with more time needed when the heater is behind a finished wall, in a tight closet, or connected to older piping.

On an electric unit, we isolate the circuit and test the thermostats and elements on the two-hundred-forty-volt system. On a gas unit, we inspect the pilot, igniter, thermocouple or flame sensor, burner assembly, vent connection, and gas control. We can often replace accessible controls, elements, valves, or connectors during the same visit when the correct part is available; a tank replacement, concealed vent correction, or special-order component is normally scheduled as separate work.

sections.heading: Tank age, shutoff, access
paragraphs: The tank age is a major factor because corrosion at the bottom seam or around a fitting can change a small repair into replacement work. A heater with a readable model plate, sound tank shell, and a failed external control is usually more straightforward to assess than a tank with rust trails, water under the jacket, or an unreadable label. The anode rod, drain valve, and threaded connections can also be harder to remove on an older appliance.

Access changes the work when the heater sits in a narrow closet, behind finished panels, on a raised platform, or beside a furnace and ductwork. A seized water shutoff can require additional valve work before we can safely isolate the appliance, and a gas control, element, or vent component that must be ordered adds a return visit. We also account for permit or sign-off requirements when replacement affects the gas line, venting, electrical connection, or water piping.

sections.heading: Model plate and access panel
paragraphs: Before calling, we ask for the model number and serial number from the manufacturer plate on the tank jacket. The plate often shows the fuel type, capacity, manufacture date, and replacement parts needed for the heater. Let us know which room holds the tank and whether it is in a closet, basement, utility room, or crawlspace. Tell us whether water is running from the relief valve, drain valve, top fittings, or the bottom seam. If the heater has a pilot or display panel, the status light pattern or error code can help us bring suitable parts. Call The Chicago Plumber at (847) 809-2341, because a leaking tank or relief valve can worsen into damaged flooring, wallboard, and nearby electrical equipment.

services.name: Faucet Repair
services.title: Faucet Repair Chicago, IL | The Chicago Plumber
services.meta: The Chicago Plumber repairs dripping, loose, noisy, and low-flow faucets in Chicago, IL. We inspect cartridges, spouts, valves, and shutoffs on site.
services.blurb: We repair dripping, loose, noisy, and low-flow faucets across Chicago.

paragraphs: Most faucet repair calls start with plain descriptions: “the sink won’t stop dripping,” “the handle is loose,” “the water barely comes out,” or “the kitchen faucet is making a noise.” We hear these calls from homeowners, landlords, tenants, and business owners dealing with a bathroom sink, kitchen faucet, utility sink, or bar fixture that no longer works as it should.

We translate the symptom into the faucet parts behind it. A drip at the spout can come from a worn cartridge, stem, seat, washer, or valve assembly. A handle that turns without changing the water may have a stripped adapter or loose set screw. Low flow can begin at the aerator, but it can also point to debris in a supply line, a damaged cartridge, or a partially closed shutoff valve below the sink.

A faucet that only drips into an empty basin can sometimes wait briefly, but a leak under the cabinet, a loose fixture, or a handle that will not shut off should not. Water escaping around the base, supply hose, or valve can damage a sink cabinet, floor, wall, and the fittings beneath the counter.

sections.heading: Drip and loose handle
paragraphs: “My faucet keeps dripping” can mean a steady stream from the spout after the handle is off, an occasional drip that starts again overnight, or water collecting around the faucet base. A spout drip usually involves the internal control parts, while water at the base may come from O-rings, a spout seal, or water traveling down from the handle.

“The handle is loose” may mean the lever moves side to side, the handle spins without changing the temperature, or the faucet body itself rocks on the sink deck. We also get calls for a faucet that whistles, bangs when it is turned on, sputters from the spout, or has a weak stream in one room while the rest of the house has normal flow.

Other common descriptions include “the hot side does not work,” “the faucet is stuck,” “the spray head leaks,” and “there is water under the sink.” The visible symptom does not reliably identify the failed part: a cartridge, retaining nut, supply hose, aerator, mounting nut, or shutoff can create similar complaints, and each fault calls for different parts and labor.

sections.heading: Cartridge and spout inspection
paragraphs: When we arrive, we start at the fixture and the cabinet below it. We run hot and cold water, check the handle travel, inspect the spout and aerator, and look for water around the escutcheon, mounting hardware, supply connections, and shutoff valves. We identify whether the faucet uses a cartridge, compression stem, ceramic disc, ball assembly, or another internal mechanism before taking it apart.

We check the water flow from each side and compare it with the fixture’s normal operation. Household water pressure commonly falls in the range of 40 to 80 psi; pressure outside that range can affect a faucet, but a single weak faucet is more often restricted at the aerator, cartridge, or supply connection. Removing an aerator and inspecting a cartridge commonly takes minutes, while a corroded retaining nut, seized handle, or faucet mounted in a tight cabinet can extend the repair.

When the needed cartridge, O-ring, aerator, hose, or mounting hardware is available, we usually complete that repair during the same visit. We clean mineral buildup, replace worn seals, secure loose hardware, test hot and cold operation, and check the cabinet for active drips. If the faucet requires a manufacturer-specific part, a specialty finish component, or replacement of the full fixture, we identify the part and arrange the next step rather than forcing an unsuitable substitute.

sections.heading: Shutoffs, cartridges, and access
paragraphs: The cartridge or stem inside the faucet is one of the main variables. Older fixtures may use parts that are worn, discontinued, or specific to a particular manufacturer and handle style. A common cartridge that can be removed cleanly is a different repair from a corroded cartridge that is bonded into the valve body or a fixture whose internal part must be matched by model.

Access under the sink also changes the work involved. A clear cabinet with working angle stops, visible supply hoses, and room for a basin wrench gives us a straightforward route to the faucet connections. A cabinet crowded with a disposal, pullout shelves, stored items, or rigid piping can make the mounting nuts and shutoffs much harder to reach.

A shutoff valve that will not close or has seized in place can add work before the faucet can be safely opened. The same applies when a supply line, mounting nut, or corroded fastener breaks during removal, or when the faucet has to be replaced because the body cannot be repaired. We explain the condition of the fixture and the required parts before moving beyond the repair that brought us to the sink.

sections.heading: Model plate and fixture location
paragraphs: Before calling, check which room contains the faucet and whether it is the kitchen sink, bathroom vanity, laundry sink, bar sink, or another fixture. If you can find a brand name or model number, take a photo of the faucet body, handle, and any model plate; model markings are often on the escutcheon, spout base, underside of the faucet, or original paperwork. Let us know roughly when the faucet was installed and whether it uses one handle, two handles, a pullout spray head, or a separate side sprayer. Tell us if water is running now, if the cabinet is wet, and whether the shutoff valves below the sink can be reached. Call The Chicago Plumber at (847) 809-2341 before a persistent drip damages the cabinet floor, supply connections, or faucet body further.

services.name: Sewer Line Repair
services.h1: Sewer Line Repair in Chicago, IL
services.title: Sewer Line Repair | The Chicago Plumber | Chicago, IL
services.meta: The Chicago Plumber handles sewer line repair in Chicago, IL, using camera inspection, cleanout testing, and clear repair planning for backups.
services.blurb: Camera-led sewer line repair for backups, odors, roots, and damaged pipe.

paragraphs: Older Chicago two-flats, brick bungalows, and buildings with original clay or cast-iron pipe can develop trouble in the sewer lateral long before a pipe is visible. Tree roots work through joints, soil can shift around buried pipe, and aging fittings may crack or separate beneath a basement floor, yard, alley, or sidewalk. We inspect sewer line problems across Chicago, Cicero, Stickney, and Oak Park, starting with the fixtures and cleanout that show where wastewater is no longer moving as it should.

A sewer line carries wastewater away from every toilet, tub, shower, sink, and floor drain connected to the building. When the lateral is blocked, damaged, or holding water, the lowest fixture often shows the first backup because gravity sends wastewater there before it rises elsewhere in the system.

A suspected sewer line fault is not work to leave waiting, especially when sewage is backing into a floor drain or basement fixture. A partial blockage can become a full stoppage, and a crack or separated joint can allow wastewater to escape into soil while roots and debris continue to close the pipe.

sections.heading: Sewage odor and gurgling drains
paragraphs: A sewage odor near a basement floor drain, utility room, or cleanout is a common reason people call us. The smell can come from wastewater sitting behind a restriction, a dry floor-drain trap, or a damaged sewer connection, so we look at the drain opening and the line condition instead of assuming the odor has one source.

Gurgling in a toilet when a washing machine drains, bubbling at a tub, or water moving in a nearby floor drain can point to a sewer line that cannot carry air and wastewater together. Those sounds may occur before a complete backup, particularly where roots have narrowed a clay-pipe joint or debris has collected at a low section of pipe.

Other callers report wastewater coming up through a basement floor drain, a toilet that will not flush while other fixtures are used, or a wet area above the buried sewer route. A single slow fixture can be a branch-drain issue, but several fixtures backing up together often directs the inspection toward the building sewer.

These symptoms can look alike from the room where they appear, yet the repair can range from an accessible cleanout issue to a broken underground pipe section. We identify the actual fault before discussing the work because the route, material, and repair scope do not carry the same cost.

sections.heading: Camera inspection and cleanout test
paragraphs: We begin at the cleanout when one is accessible, then check the basement floor drain, toilets, and other fixtures involved in the backup. The cleanout is often a capped pipe near the basement wall or utility area; its opening lets us test the sewer route without removing a toilet or opening a finished wall.

A camera inspection commonly takes about 30 to 60 minutes once the line can be accessed, although a line holding wastewater or packed with roots can require more preparation. We feed the camera through the cleanout, view the interior of the pipe, and check for roots, grease, offset joints, cracks, standing water, collapsed sections, or a foreign object. We also identify the visible pipe material, such as clay, cast iron, or PVC, and measure the likely location of a defect from the access point.

Where the line can be opened and the problem is reachable through the cleanout, we may be able to clear the obstruction and complete the camera check during the same visit. A broken lateral, a section beneath concrete, or pipe that needs excavation is normally planned as separate work so the route, access, replacement material, and any required site preparation can be set out properly.

For a localized damaged section, the repair may involve removing the failed pipe and installing new pipe with properly aligned fittings. When the camera shows repeated root entry or several separated joints, we discuss whether a spot repair addresses the condition or whether a longer section of the sewer route needs attention.

sections.heading: Pipe depth and yard access
paragraphs: The buried pipe route and its depth strongly affect the repair scope. A sewer lateral beneath an open yard is approached differently from one that runs under a concrete basement slab, garage floor, sidewalk, porch, alley, or landscaped area with fences and mature roots.

Pipe age and material also matter. Older clay pipe can fail at individual joints, while aging cast iron may develop internal scale, corrosion, or cracks along more than one section. A camera image helps show whether the repair is confined to one break or whether the line has deterioration beyond the first blockage.

Access at the cleanout can change the amount of investigation needed before repair begins. A seized cleanout cap, a buried cleanout, or a line with no usable access point may require additional work to reach the pipe safely and inspect the full route.

Replacement material availability and the need for a permit, utility marking, or inspection sign-off can also affect scheduling and scope. We explain which portion of the line is visible on the camera, what access is available, and what work must be planned before a buried pipe section is opened.

sections.heading: Cleanout location and pipe material
paragraphs: Before calling, check whether you can locate a sewer cleanout cap in the basement, utility room, crawlspace, yard, or near the building wall. If an exposed pipe section is visible, note whether it appears to be clay, cast iron, PVC, or another material, and whether any cap or fitting is leaking.

Tell us which room has the backup and which fixtures are involved, especially if wastewater is rising through a basement floor drain. If you know when the building was built or when the sewer pipe was last replaced, that age can help us plan the camera route and likely pipe material.

Let us know whether wastewater is standing now and whether the cleanout, basement, yard gate, alley, or exterior pipe route is accessible. Call The Chicago Plumber at (847) 809-2341 before a partial sewer blockage becomes a basement-floor-drain backup with wastewater spreading across the floor.

home.aboutHeading: A Local Plumbing Company in Chicago, IL
about: We work from 210 N Racine Ave in Chicago, IL, and cover plumbing calls across Chicago, Cicero, Stickney, and Oak Park. Our crews travel from this Racine Avenue address to homes, apartments, storefronts, and other properties throughout the area.

We take on drain cleaning, leak repair, toilet repair, water heater repair, faucet repair, and sewer line repair. We repair and replace fixtures, pipes, drains, water heaters, and sewer lines in kitchens, bathrooms, basements, utility rooms, and exterior areas.

At a visit, we start by looking at the fixture, pipe, drain, shutoff valve, water heater, or sewer access involved. We check the visible condition and affected component before discussing money, repair work, or replacement options.
